Tex. 2014) -- a functionally identical clone of the card game Bang! with different art/theme did NOT infringe: 'game mechanics and the rules are not entitled to protection,' including the roles-and-interactions structure (Sheriff/Deputy/Outlaw/Renegade -- directly analogous to Town/Mafia/Neutral role structures) (https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/texas-court-affirms-game-mechanics-not-protected-under-copyright-law, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-txsd-4_13-cv-03415/pdf/USCOURTS-txsd-4_13-cv-03415-0.pdf). Spry Fox v. LOLApps (W.D. Wash. 2012) -- the cautionary middle case: court excluded functional elements (6x6 grid) and scenes-a-faire (coins as score) but held the overall selection/arrangement of expressive elements plus closely-mapped theme (bear->yeti, bush->sapling) could state a claim; aggravated by the defendant having had NDA access. Lesson: don't do a 1:1 reskin where every expressive element has an obvious counterpart, and don't copy the 'total concept and feel' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spry_Fox,_LLC_v._Lolapps,_Inc.). --- LAYER 3, the underlying game is public domain: Mafia/Werewolf was created by Dimitry Davidoff at Moscow State University in 1986 and has been freely reimplemented for decades (Werewolf variant by Andrew Plotkin 1997); nobody owns day/night, lynching, or informed-minority-vs-uninformed-majority (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafia_(party_game)). --- THE KEY PRECEDENT, Town of Salem: BlankMediaGames' Town of Salem (Steam, Dec 2014) is openly and admittedly based on SC2Mafia -- community sources confirm 'Town of Salem is based off of SC2:Mafia' and SC2Mafia's creator Dark.Revenant even helped promote it (http://www.sc2mafia.com/forum/archive/index.php/t-25658.html, https://steamcommunity.com/app/334230/discussions/0/610573009238451786/). ToS kept the day/night/trial structure, the faction layout, the role MECHANICS, and even dozens of literal ROLE NAMES from SC2Mafia (Jailor, Veteran, Escort, Consort, Lookout, Spy, Blackmailer, Framer, Janitor, Disguiser, Consigliere, Mafioso, Godfather, Bodyguard, Investigator, Witch, Arsonist, Serial Killer, Jester, Executioner, Amnesiac, Survivor...) -- it changed the name, the theme (Salem witch trials), and all art/audio/text, and it shipped commercially for a decade with zero Blizzard action. A second-generation precedent exists too: Throne of Lies and other ToS-likes shipped fine on Steam. --- ROLE NAMES analysis: copyright does not protect names, titles, or short phrases at all (US Copyright Office Circular 33), so role names are only ever a trademark/trade-dress question, and neither Blizzard nor BMG has trademarked individual role names. Generic tier (predates SC2Mafia in the broader Mafia community -- MafiaScum/EpicMafia used Cop/Sheriff, Doctor, Vigilante, Godfather, Mayor, Jester, Serial Killer, Survivor, Mason long before 2010): zero risk. Middle tier (popularized by SC2Mafia, copied wholesale by Town of Salem: Jailor, Escort/Consort, Veteran, Lookout, Consigliere, Framer, Janitor, Blackmailer, Disguiser, Witch, Arsonist, Executioner, Amnesiac): very low risk -- ToS itself proves these traveled freely, and as single descriptive words they're unprotectable; copying the ENTIRE list verbatim with identical descriptions edges toward a selection-and-arrangement claim (Spry Fox), so vary the lineup and write all descriptions fresh. Distinctive tier (SC2Mafia-specific flavor, esp. the Triad faction's Chinese-themed names -- Dragon Head, Incense Master, Vanguard, Enforcer, Administrator, Silencer, Informant, Liaison, Sweeper -- plus oddballs like Beguiler/Auditor): these are SC2Mafia's recognizable creative fingerprint; individually still just short phrases, but reproducing the whole distinctive set signals copying and invites a look-and-feel argument -- rename or re-theme these. --- BOTTOM LINE RISK: a clean-room clone with original name/art/text/theme that reuses the mechanics and the generic-to-middle-tier role vocabulary sits squarely in DaVinci v. ZiKo safe territory, is exactly what Town of Salem already did commercially without incident, and the realistic Blizzard risk is approximately zero provided no StarCraft marks/assets appear anywhere. The marginally larger practical risk is actually a look-and-feel complaint from BlankMediaGames if the clone reads as a Town-of-Salem reskin -- so differentiate theme/UI from ToS as well as from SC2.
mustChange: The name 'SC2Mafia' -- 'SC2' invokes Blizzard's StarCraft trademark; pick a wholly original title (also check USPTO/Steam for collisions, and note 'Mafia' alone collides with 2K's Mafia franchise trademark for video games -- safer as part of a longer distinctive mark or avoided)
Any StarCraft II assets: unit models/portraits used as character avatars, Blizzard sound effects, music, UI textures, fonts, icons -- all Blizzard property, zero tolerance

Any code or data exported from the map: Galaxy script, trigger logic, the map file, data tables -- Blizzard claims ownership of the map's contents under the Custom Game AUP; reimplement from observed behavior (clean-room), never from extracted files

All verbatim text from SC2Mafia: role descriptions, help/tutorial text, flavor text, investigator result strings, death announcements -- rewrite everything from scratch even where the underlying fact conveyed is the same

References to Blizzard, Battle.net, StarCraft, or Arcade anywhere in the game, store page, or marketing; do not market it as 'SC2Mafia on Steam' (nominative references in press interviews about inspiration are fine; trading on the mark in the product is not)
The SC2Mafia logo and any community-made art associated with the map

The distinctive SC2Mafia-specific role-name set, especially the Triad faction's themed names (Dragon Head, Incense Master, Vanguard, Enforcer, Administrator, Silencer, Informant, Liaison, Sweeper) and oddball original names (e.g. Beguiler, Auditor) -- rename or re-theme; these are the map's creative fingerprint

Avoid a 1:1 expressive mapping (Spry Fox lesson): don't reproduce the exact full role list, exact setup lists, and exact UI layout simultaneously -- vary the lineup, add original roles, design an original visual theme distinct from BOTH StarCraft and Town of Salem's Salem-witch-trial trade dress
Original visual identity overall: character art, setting/theme, UI design, color language, sound -- the 'total look and feel' is where Tetris v. Xio says clones actually lose
safeToKeep: The core Mafia/Werewolf framework itself: hidden roles, informed minority vs uninformed majority, day/night cycle -- public domain party game (Davidoff 1986), unprotectable rules
Day/night phase structure with timed phases, night actions resolved simultaneously, day discussion
Voting, trial, defense statement, and lynch mechanics (vote to put on trial, defense speech, guilty/innocent vote) -- pure mechanics under DaVinci v. ZiKo / 17 USC 102(b)
Faction structure: Town vs Mafia vs a second evil faction vs Neutrals, with faction win conditions -- role-interaction structure explicitly held unprotectable in DaVinci v. ZiKo

Role MECHANICS as behaviors: investigate alignment, heal/protect, roleblock, jail-and-execute, douse-then-ignite, witch-control, bus-drive/swap, frame, clean death, disguise, last-will notes, whispers, death notes -- mechanics are ideas, not expression

Generic role names with pre-SC2Mafia community provenance: Sheriff, Doctor, Investigator/Detective, Vigilante, Mayor, Bodyguard, Godfather, Mafioso, Jester, Serial Killer, Survivor, Witch, Mason -- standard Mafia-genre vocabulary (scenes-a-faire), used across MafiaScum/EpicMafia/Town of Salem/Town of Salem 2 without incident

Middle-tier role names popularized by SC2Mafia and already freely propagated through Town of Salem (Jailor, Veteran, Escort, Lookout, Consigliere, Framer, Janitor, Blackmailer, Disguiser, Arsonist, Executioner, Amnesiac) -- individually safe as unprotectable short phrases; just don't clone the entire roster verbatim with identical descriptions
Lobby/host model: 15-player named lobbies, host-configurable role lists, repick/host migration -- functional design, fully reimplementable
Game-flow conventions: graveyard with revealed roles, last words, whisper system, day chat / mafia night chat split -- functional/scenes-a-faire for the genre

Marketing truthfully in interviews/devlogs that the game is 'inspired by the classic Mafia party game' and by the SC2 Arcade community scene -- factual statements, nominative fair use; just keep marks out of the title/store assets

games.name: Town of Salem (2014)
games.stack: Originally Adobe Flash browser client + Steam wrapper; custom PHP/phpBB web backend (the forum software became the breach vector). Ported to Unity 2019-2020 when Flash died: Steam Unity client Oct 28, 2019; browser client re-released as Unity WebGL May 28, 2020. Funded by a $17,190 Kickstarter (Feb 2014, $15k goal); released Dec 15, 2014. Mobile (Unity) Oct 2018.
games.outcome: Player lifecycle: huge web population (7.6M+ registered accounts by 2018) plus Steam all-time peak 3,687 CCU (Jan 2018). Dec 2018: data breach of 7.6M accounts (>95% of registered users) via phpBB forum vulnerabilities + admin password reuse; exposed usernames, emails, weakly-hashed (MD5/phpass-class) passwords — 27% cracked quickly — IPs, partial payment data. Breach went unacknowledged until Jan 2019; attackers persisted in the network for an extended period and compromised creds still authenticated months later (inadequate forced resets); likely GDPR violations. Weeks before the breach disclosure (Nov 3, 2018) the free web version moved to a paid model, officially to combat spam/bot attacks. The game is still alive 11+ years on but tiny: ~97 CCU current, ~101 30-day average (June 2026), stable in the 90s. Sustained by: cheap one-time price (~$4.99) + Coven DLC (2017) + cosmetic Town Points economy, and by being the canonical browser-accessible Mafia implementation for years. Sources: haveibeenpwned.com/breach/blankmediagames, bleepingcomputer.com 27%-cracked article, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_of_Salem, steamcharts.com/app/334230.
lessons: Forum/CMS software bolted onto a game account database is an attack surface: phpBB, shared admin passwords, and weak hashing turned a small indie into a 7.6M-account breach.
Slow disclosure (breach Dec 13, discovered publicly via DeHashed in Jan) and not forcing password resets did lasting reputation damage that outweighed the technical fix.
Engine-platform risk is real: betting on Flash forced a full Unity rewrite mid-life; the rewrite consumed dev capacity that could have gone to content.
Switching a F2P web game to paid (anti-bot rationale) cut off the new-player funnel that deduction games depend on.
A 15-player deduction game can survive a decade at ~100 CCU if matchmaking pools concentrate in a few modes and the price of keeping servers up is low.

games.name: Town of Salem 2 (2023)
games.stack: Unity, BlankMediaGames LLC. Early Access on Steam May 26, 2023; 1.0 Aug 25, 2023. Later on Epic Games Store (free-game-of-the-week promotion April 2024) and mobile (iOS app late 2023).
games.outcome: Launched paid; all-time Steam peak only 3,022-3,755 CCU (May/June 2023) — i.e., the sequel never exceeded the original's 2018 peak. Sharp 26.9% drop June→July 2023. Went free-to-play Sept 15, 2023 with an energy-gate: free players get 1 'key' per 8 hours (max 5 banked), one key per match; pre-F2P buyers got a 'Super Deed' unlock. F2P did NOT recover the population — recent-review sentiment fell to ~40% positive, with complaints about ramped-up MTX including the Cauldron loot box with gacha mechanics, and 'less playercount than launch even after going free to play.' Current state: ~263-333 CCU, ~273 30-day average (June 2026). Community threads titled 'Town of Salem 2 is on its way out.' Sources: steamcharts.com/app/2140510, steamcommunity.com F2P announcement and discussions.
lessons: A sequel splits an already-small deduction population across two games; ToS1 + ToS2 combined are under 400 CCU.
Energy/key gating is poison for a genre that needs warm bodies in lobbies — limiting free matches directly starves matchmaking.
Going F2P after charging early adopters generated resentment twice: buyers felt burned, free players felt nickel-and-dimed by loot boxes.
F2P conversion cannot resurrect a game whose population already fell below the matchmaking-viability threshold; the funnel must be open from day one.

games.name: Among Us (2018)
games.stack: Unity (C#), Innersloth (3-5 person team at launch). Custom lightweight networking ('Hazel' UDP library); architecture was lobby-host-authoritative (one player's client runs game logic) with Innersloth relay/matchmaking servers — effectively peer-hosted logic. Free on iOS/Android, $4.99 on Steam (June 2018 PC). After the 2020 explosion Innersloth partnered with Unity: Multiplay hybrid dedicated-server hosting (30+ bare-metal providers + 4 clouds, 99.95% SLA), Unity Analytics, Vivox. Connected 500M+ lifetime players on this infra.
games.outcome: Near-dead at launch (double-digit CCU through 2018-2019; Innersloth kept updating anyway). Mid-2020: Twitch/YouTube streamers ignited it; featured on Steam Aug 2020; >1M DAU, doubling in 9 days, eventually 8-digit DAU; ~500M MAU at the Nov 2020 peak; Steam all-time peak 438,524 CCU (Sept 2020). Revenue: $24.5M in Oct 2020 alone; ~$86M in first three years; $100M+ lifetime — from a $5 PC price plus mobile cosmetics/ads. Cheating crisis Oct 2020: 'Eris Loris' spam attack hit ~1.5M games / ~5M players (pro-Trump + YouTube-sub spam) by exploiting the trust-the-host/client architecture; emergency server update pushed; accelerated server-authority work. Free mobile + no accounts made ban evasion trivial, so: Quick Chat for accountless guests, full account system March 31, 2021 (free chat requires account; bans extend to alts), cross-device accounts Nov 2021, plus in-game reporting categories. Long tail: ~20M MAU and 2.5-2.9M DAU in 2025; Steam ~7.2k 30-day average CCU, ~10k current, monthly peaks ~20k (early 2026) — cyclical spikes with updates/sales. Among Us 3D launched 2025 as a separate SKU. Sources: unity.com/resources/innersloth-among-us, multiplayunity.medium.com case study, kotaku.com & engadget.com Eris Loris coverage, among-us.fandom.com/wiki/Account, steamcharts.com/app/945360, blog.udonis.co player-count report.
lessons: Peer-hosted/host-authoritative networking is fine for 50 CCU and catastrophic at 1M DAU: no server validation meant one person with a dozen volunteers could spam 1.5M lobbies.
Account systems can be retrofitted (took ~6 months) but moderation debt compounds; guest-mode-with-Quick-Chat was the pragmatic bridge for child safety + ban evasion.
Streamability (simple visuals, 10-player lobbies, betrayal moments) is the single biggest acquisition channel this genre has; the game changed nothing in 2020 — streamers found it.
Keep shipping while dead: Among Us survived two years of obscurity because the team was tiny and costs were near zero.
$5 one-time on PC + free-with-cosmetics mobile monetized 500M players without poisoning goodwill; they cancelled Among Us 2 and reinvested in the original.
Buying scaling (Unity Multiplay) instead of building it let a 5-person team survive a 10,000x load spike.

games.name: Throne of Lies: Medieval Politics (2017)
games.stack: Unity 3D, Imperium42 (husband-and-wife founders Dylan & Elsa Hunt, Las Vegas/Taiwan). Kickstarter Jan-Feb 2017: $21,795 from 393 backers ($20k goal). Launched Steam Sept 2017 at $9.99; upgraded to Unity 2018 mid-life (introduced gamebreaking bugs); F2P relaunch Dec 23, 2020.
games.outcome: ~500k activations lifetime; all-time peak just 1,381-1,382 CCU (May 2019). Single active developer on an indie budget; activity concentrated into one daily window (~7pm EST) as population shrank. F2P relaunch in Dec 2020 — riding the Among Us wave — failed to flourish. Community cited heavy-handed community management as a retention factor. Current: 30-day average ~1.2 CCU, peaks of ~13 (June 2026) — functionally dead, servers still up. Sources: steamcharts.com/app/595280, kickstarter.com Imperium42 campaign, gamespress.com F2P announcement, steamcommunity.com app/595280 discussions.
lessons: $10 paid entry + niche theme + small marketing = never reached critical mass; the all-time peak (~1.4k) was already marginal for 10-16-player lobbies.
When CCU drops, surviving communities self-organize into scheduled play windows — a death-spiral symptom worth instrumenting for.
F2P conversion done after the population collapsed recovers nothing (same lesson as ToS2).
Moderation style is a retention variable: in small communities, perceived unfair community management churns the regulars who keep lobbies alive.
3D production values added cost but not retention vs. 2D competitors.

games.name: Feign (2021)
games.stack: Unity (PC + Android/iOS), Turkish studio Teneke Kafalar, later published with Kwalee. Built-in lobby voice chat. Steam Early Access Oct 23, 2021 at ~€4.99 (~$5); $1.99 on Android. 12-player Innocents/Impostors/Neutrals format with werewolf-style night roles.
games.outcome: Modest but unusually durable mid-tail: all-time peak 2,688 CCU (Dec 2021), and still ~97-150 CCU with spikes to ~434 in June 2026 — i.e., four-plus years later it retains a higher share of its peak than most genre peers. Periodic resurgences (Nov 2025 +77% month) track Turkish streamer waves; very strong regional (Turkey) identity and 14-language localization. ~4,810 Steam reviews, 91% positive. Sources: steamcharts.com/app/1436990, store.steampowered.com/app/1436990, tenekekafalar.com/feign.html, steamspy.com/app/1436990.
lessons: Owning one regional/language community (Turkey) gives a small deduction game a defensible lobby population that global also-rans lack.
Built-in voice chat keeps casual groups inside the game instead of fragmenting into Discord-only private lobbies.
Cheap one-time price (~$5) with high review score sustains a slow steady funnel; recurring streamer spikes re-seed the population.
A 12-player game idling at ~100 CCU concentrated in one region/timezone still fills lobbies; the same 100 CCU spread globally would not.

games.name: Goose Goose Duck (2021)
games.stack: Unity, Gaggle Studios (NY). Free-to-play from launch (Oct 2021). Built-in voice chat including proximity voice — its key differentiator vs Among Us. Easy Anti-Cheat added to combat ESP/speedhack cheats. Monetization: cosmetics + 'Flight Pass' battle pass; ~$21.5M revenue in 2024. Separate China mobile version launched Jan 2026 (crashed on day one under load).
games.outcome: The genre's second viral event: BTS member Kim Taehyung (V) streamed it Nov 2022 → explosion in China → Steam servers crashed twice under the surge → all-time peak 701,898-703,000 Steam CCU (Jan 12, 2023), beating Among Us's Steam record; ~800k CCU including mobile. Chinese streaming platforms restricted GGD streams after players used politically sensitive handles (Jan 2023). Post-peak decline was steep but landed on a real plateau: ~40k peak Jan 2024, ~37k Oct 2024, ~8.3k current / ~3.9k 30-day average with 13k monthly peaks (June 2026) — still the second-most-populated game in the genre. Sustained by constant cosmetic events, the battle pass, voice-first casual play, and the China mobile launch. Sources: gamedeveloper.com 800k article, dualshockers.com record article, newsletter.gamediscover.co/p/how-goose-goose-duck-hit-700k-ccu, steamcharts.com/app/1568590, technode.com China-launch article, rfa.org stream-restriction article.
lessons: F2P + built-in proximity voice out-executed the incumbent: zero price friction plus not needing Discord captured the casual wave Among Us created.
Celebrity/streamer ignition (one BTS stream) can 100x a population overnight — and infrastructure must absorb it or the moment is wasted (servers crashed twice; they apologized and scaled).
China concentration is high-beta: it created the record peak, brought platform-censorship interference, and its retreat caused most of the crash; they re-bet on it with a localized mobile launch.
F2P deduction games attract industrial-scale cheating (public ESP/radar tools); EAC became necessary — a cost paid only because the game was big enough to matter.
Live-ops cadence (events, Flight Pass, cosmetics) is what separated its ~$21.5M/yr plateau from peers that fell to double-digit CCU.

games.name: Project Winter (2019)
games.stack: Unity, Other Ocean Interactive (established work-for-hire studio). Paid title (~$19.99) + cosmetic DLC packs (e.g., Blackout DLC); released May 23, 2019 after Early Access; Xbox Game Pass (2021) with crossplay; Switch port. 8-player survival + social deception hybrid with integrated voice chat (proximity + radio). Partnered with Modulate to trial ToxMod ML voice moderation after acknowledging rising toxicity.
games.outcome: Steady mid-size population for years (peaks ~2,865 CCU as late as Aug 30, 2024; Game Pass drove console/crossplay population). Notable as an early adopter of automated voice moderation — devs publicly posted 'Addressing Community Toxicity' and deployed ToxMod trials because voice-first deception games concentrate abuse. Despite a 2025 roadmap and a 'Cabin Fever / Project Winter 2.0' relaunch attempt (Sept 2025, brief spike to ~686 avg), population collapsed: ~11-14 CCU, -48% month-over-month (June 2026) — below matchmaking viability for an 8-player game. Sources: steambase.io/games/project-winter/steam-charts, store.steampowered.com/news/app/774861 (toxicity post, 2025 roadmap), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Winter, trueachievements.com Game Pass coverage.
lessons: Survival-mechanics + deduction hybrid raises match length and skill floor, shrinking the casual funnel the genre needs.
Voice-required deception gameplay concentrates toxicity; Other Ocean's ToxMod partnership shows the moderation burden is heavy enough that studios outsource it to ML.
Game Pass inclusion buys population temporarily but it evaporates when the catalog rotates.
A '2.0' relaunch update (Sept 2025) produced only a one-month spike — content drops cannot fix a structurally depleted matchmaking pool.
$20 price point is hostile to the 'bring 7 friends' acquisition loop this genre runs on.

games.name: Blood on the Clocktower — official digital (botc.app)
games.stack: Browser-based web app (Windows/Mac/Linux, all major browsers), official app developed under The Pandemonium Institute; release repo on GitHub (ThePandemoniumInstitute/botc-release). Integrated audio/video: microphone required, camera optional. No matchmaking algorithm — games are human-run: a Storyteller (referee with full grimoire access and private-chat visibility) hosts public or private (link/code) games; spectator seats; private whisper chats with neighbor animations; hand-raising for nominations.
games.outcome: Long Patreon-gated beta ('under construction' for years, community 'arriving early'); now free to play with optional Patreon membership unlocking avatar cosmetics and supporting development; Patreon also gates the official Discord/early access. The digital app deliberately complements a premium physical product (~$130+ board game) rather than replacing it. Coexists with a free open-source unofficial tool, clocktower.online (bra1n/townsquare on GitHub) — a virtual grimoire/town square used with Discord/Zoom voice — which the publisher tolerates. Population is not Steam-trackable but the game's online community (Patreon, Discord, public game listings across languages/difficulties) is active and growing; the BGG consensus treats it as the best-in-class social deduction design. Key structural difference: every game needs a trained human Storyteller, which caps scale but near-eliminates the dead-lobby and moderation problems — the Storyteller is the moderator. Sources: botc.app, release.botc.app, beardytas.com/botc-app-instructions, patreon.com/cw/botconline, github.com/bra1n/townsquare, bloodontheclocktower.com.
lessons: Human-hosted games (Storyteller model) trade scalability for quality: no matchmaking death spiral because games are scheduled social events, and moderation is built into the role.
Free digital app as marketing for a premium physical game + Patreon-for-cosmetics is a viable model that avoids MTX resentment entirely.
Web-native (browser + WebRTC-style AV) removes install friction for a 10-20 player game where one reluctant friend not installing kills the night.
Tolerating a free open-source community tool (clocktower.online) grew the online scene during the years the official app wasn't ready.
Patreon-gated beta built a paying community before launch and funded multi-year development without a publisher.

games.name: EpicMafia (2008) → UltiMafia
games.stack: EpicMafia: custom web app (live chat-based mafia), created Jan 2008, run by 'lucidrains'; volunteer moderators; free. Successor UltiMafia (fork launched June 12, 2023): open-source MERN stack — React frontend, Node.js/Express with websockets, MongoDB + Redis — github.com/UltiMafia/Ultimafia, volunteer-run, free, community-driven with deep role/setup customization.
games.outcome: EpicMafia ran 13 years as the definitive browser mafia site and the proving ground for competitive setups (Town of Salem borrowed heavily from this lineage). It died socially, not technically: in March 2021 moderators were outed for predatory/pedophilic behavior; a moderator ('Charley') self-deleted after deleting banned users' posts, completing a collapse of governance; owner lucidrains shut the site permanently on March 20, 2021, refusing buyout offers. Community recreations followed; UltiMafia is the active successor as of 2025, sustained by open-source contributors and volunteer moderation. Sources: epicmafia.fandom.com/wiki/The_Death_of_EpicMafia, github.com/UltiMafia/Ultimafia, ultimafia.com.
lessons: Anonymous-volunteer moderation with absentee ownership is an existential risk: EpicMafia was killed by moderator misconduct and governance collapse, not by technology or population loss.
Long-lived deduction communities accumulate child-safety liability — text chat + minors + anonymous adults requires real trust-and-safety, even for a hobby site.
A devoted community will rebuild the platform (UltiMafia, open-source) if the code/concept is replicable — the durable asset is the ruleset and community, not the site.
MERN + websockets is entirely sufficient tech for text-based real-time mafia; the hard part is governance.
Refusing to sell and hard-killing the site destroyed 13 years of community capital overnight — succession planning matters for community platforms.

games.name: werewolf.chat (lykos IRC) / Mafia.gg / werewolv.es — small web implementations
games.stack: werewolf.chat: MediaWiki documentation hub for 'lykos', an open-source Werewolf IRC bot (Python, GitHub); games run in #werewolf on irc.libera.chat and other IRC networks — pure text, zero hosting cost beyond the bot. Mafia.gg: free browser SPA (JS client-rendered; page serves no static content to crawlers) offering real-time lobbies, chat, role customization, spectating, host controls for private groups. werewolv.es: free browser Werewolf with live community games, long-form and 'turbo' formats. Also Discord-bot mafia and forum mafia (e.g., Mafia Universe community) as adjacent zero-infrastructure formats.
games.outcome: These survive indefinitely at tiny scale because their costs round to zero and their communities self-host the social layer. lykos's wiki shows only moderate activity (last notable edit 2023) but the IRC games continue across multiple networks; leaderboards and quote databases indicate an entrenched micro-community. Mafia.gg persists as a private-group tool — players bring their own group, so it has no matchmaking-pool problem. None monetize meaningfully; none died of population collapse because they never depended on strangers-matchmaking. Sources: werewolf.chat (lykos wiki), mafia.gg, werewolv.es, forums.online-go.com forum-werewolf threads.
lessons: Bring-your-own-group tools are immune to the population death spiral — the existential risk of matchmade deduction games simply doesn't apply.
Text-only/IRC/Discord-bot implementations prove the genre's floor cost is ~zero; a web deduction game competes against free forever.
Hostable private-lobby tooling (role customization, host controls, spectating) is the feature set that retains organized communities.
These platforms cap out small: no onboarding funnel for strangers means no growth, the mirror image of the matchmade games' problem.

comps.monetization: What worked: (1) Cheap one-time purchase on PC + free mobile with cosmetics — Among Us's $4.99 + cosmetics/ads/Stars currency generated $86M in three years and $100M+ lifetime with near-zero goodwill damage; the low price preserved the 'convince 9 friends to buy it' loop. (2) F2P from day one + cosmetics + battle pass + built-in voice — Goose Goose Duck rode zero price friction to a 703k CCU record and still cleared ~$21.5M in 2024 on cosmetics and its Flight Pass, funding the live-ops cadence that keeps it the #2 survivor. (3) Free digital client as a funnel for a premium physical product + Patreon patronage for cosmetics/early access — Blood on the Clocktower's botc.app is free, monetizing fandom rather than gameplay, with human Storytellers eliminating per-match server-moderation costs. (4) Modest price + strong regional community — Feign's ~$5 sustains a small studio off one loyal market. What poisoned the well: ToS2's late F2P pivot with an energy/key system (1 free match-key per 8 hours) plus gacha loot boxes ('Cauldron') — energy gates directly starve the lobby population the genre lives on, and converting paid early adopters to F2P-with-MTX burned both audiences (40% positive recent reviews). Charging $10-20 upfront for an unknown deduction game (Throne of Lies at $9.99, Project Winter at $19.99) suppressed the initial population below critical mass; both games' later F2P/relaunch attempts failed because conversion after the pool collapses recovers nothing. ToS1's switch of its free web client to paid (Nov 2018, anti-bot rationale) closed its funnel. Pattern: monetization must never gate match participation or group acquisition; cosmetics, patronage, and a sub-$5 entry are the only models with surviving examples.
pitfalls: Population death spiral: deduction needs 7-16 players per lobby, so matchmade games have a hard CCU floor (~a few hundred globally, less if concentrated in one timezone). Below it, queues lengthen, casuals leave, and collapse is self-reinforcing — Throne of Lies (1.4k peak → 1 CCU), Project Winter (2.9k → 11), ToS2 (~3k → ~270). Symptoms appear early as 'the game is only alive at 7pm EST' scheduling.
Sequels and spin-offs cannibalize the same fixed pool: ToS1+ToS2 combined hold under 400 CCU; Innersloth cancelled Among Us 2 and reinvested in the original — the correct call.

Cheating amplified by friends-in-voice-chat and client trust: Among Us's host-authoritative/peer-hosted architecture let the Eris Loris attack spam ~1.5M lobbies in three days; F2P titles (GGD) attract commercial ESP/radar/speedhack tools requiring Easy Anti-Cheat; private-info leakage via out-of-band Discord voice is unsolvable technically and must be absorbed by design (built-in voice, proximity chat, private-lobby culture).

Free accounts = trivial ban evasion: Among Us needed Quick Chat for guests, then a full account system (Mar 2021) with alt-account bans; ToS1 made its web version paid specifically against bot/spam floods. Plan identity/abuse infrastructure before going F2P.

Account security and web-stack debt: ToS1's 7.6M-account breach came from phpBB forum software, admin password reuse, weak hashing, slow disclosure, and no forced resets — the company nearly defined GDPR-era negligence for indies. Any auxiliary web surface (forums, wikis) shares blast radius with the game DB.

Toxicity/moderation burden scales worse in voice-first deception games: Project Winter publicly partnered with Modulate ToxMod (ML voice moderation); werewolf communities burn out volunteer mods. EpicMafia is the terminal case — the site died in 2021 from moderator predatory misconduct and governance collapse, not load or money. Text+minors+anonymous adults = real trust-and-safety obligations.

Virality is also a stress event: GGD's Steam servers crashed twice during its BTS/China surge and its China mobile launch crashed on day one; capacity must be elastic (Among Us bought Unity Multiplay rather than building).
Geo-concentration risk: GGD's record peak was mostly China and so was its crash; Chinese platforms restricted its streams over politically sensitive player handles.

Engine/platform mortality: Flash EOL forced ToS1's full Unity rewrite; Throne of Lies's Unity 2018 upgrade shipped gamebreaking bugs. Mid-life engine migrations consume the content budget that retention requires.
Energy gates, loot boxes, or any pay-per-match friction directly attack lobby liquidity — ToS2's key system is the canonical self-inflicted wound.
successFactors: Streamability is the genre's acquisition engine: Among Us 2020 (Twitch) and Goose Goose Duck 2022-23 (one BTS member's stream) were both ignited by streamers, not marketing. Design for spectacle: readable 2D art, betrayal reveals, short rounds, clippable moments. Feign's periodic Turkish-streamer waves repeatedly re-seed its population.

Built-in voice (especially proximity voice) is now table stakes: GGD's voice-first design out-executed Among Us; Feign and Project Winter shipped it; BotC requires a mic. It keeps casual groups in-game instead of losing them to Discord and lowers the friend-group assembly cost.
Survive the quiet years cheaply: Among Us's 3-5-person team kept shipping for two dead years before the explosion; ToS1 persists 11 years at ~100 CCU because costs are tiny. Low burn is a strategy.

Buy infrastructure, don't build: Unity Multiplay (30+ bare-metal + 4 cloud providers, 99.95% SLA) absorbed Among Us's 10,000x spike for a team of five; GGD scaled after crashing; the lesson is elastic capacity ready before the viral moment.
Live-ops cadence sustains the plateau: GGD's events/cosmetics/Flight Pass keep it at thousands of CCU and ~$21.5M/yr while content-starved peers fell to double digits.

Bring-your-own-group and human-hosted models are death-spiral-proof: BotC's Storyteller-run scheduled games, Mafia.gg/Discord-bot private lobbies, and IRC lykos games never depend on stranger matchmaking — they cap small but never die. A hybrid (matchmaking + first-class private/community hosting tools) hedges the population risk.

Community ownership extends life beyond the company: open-source UltiMafia (MERN) resurrected EpicMafia's community; clocktower.online (open-source grimoire) carried BotC online before the official app. Moddability/hostability converts players into infrastructure.

Regional/language community depth beats shallow global reach for small titles: Feign's Turkey-centric population fills lobbies at CCU levels that would be fatal if globally dispersed; localization (14 languages) is cheap insurance.
Zero or near-zero entry price keeps the group-acquisition loop alive: every surviving title is free or under $5; every $10+ title in the genre is dead.

Account systems, reporting, and (for voice games) ML moderation tooling are retention features, not compliance overhead — toxicity churns exactly the casual majority the lobbies need; Among Us's accounts/Quick Chat and Project Winter's ToxMod trial mark the genre's minimum bar.

topRisks.risk: Population cold-start is the existential risk and the dossier documents it without solving it. A 15-player lobby needs roughly 10x the concurrent pool of Among Us's 4-10 player rooms; the dossier's own comps show every matchmade deduction game under ~300 CCU is functionally dead (Throne of Lies 1.4k peak -> 1 CCU, Project Winter 2.9k -> 11). A text-only clone of a 2011 SC2 Arcade map launches with zero acquisition channel: no streamer appeal, no marketing budget, no existing funnel. The most likely failure mode is launching to empty lobbies, collecting 'can't find a game' Steam reviews that are permanent, and spiraling within 4-8 weeks.
topRisks.mitigation: Design out dependence on stranger matchmaking: make bring-your-own-group private lobbies the first-class mode (the dossier's own werewolf.chat/Mafia.gg lesson — BYO-group tools are death-spiral-immune); support 7-15 players with auto-scaling role lists so a 9-person lobby starts instead of waiting; recruit the SC2Mafia diaspora, UltiMafia, and Discord mafia communities as founding hosts BEFORE launch; ship scheduled-event tooling (community game nights) instead of pretending a quickmatch queue will fill; launch the free browser client months before Steam to build the pool, and only pull the Steam launch trigger when there's a measurable nightly population.

topRisks.risk: Solo-dev playtest impossibility is the hidden schedule killer. Every balance/UX iteration of a 15-player, 30-60 minute game requires 10-15 simultaneous humans; that throttles iteration to maybe two real sessions a week, and the genre's fun lives entirely in emergent multi-player dynamics no unit test reaches. The dossier never addresses how one person tests this game at all.
topRisks.mitigation: Build the deterministic headless simulator and scripted bot clients on day one — the dossier's own (seed, intents) -> deterministic-resolution design enables this; add property-based and golden-case tests for the night-resolution pipeline; run 1-human-plus-14-bots smoke tests for every flow; use Steam Playtest (free, separate app, missing from the dossier's shipping steps) plus a standing Discord playtest group with scheduled sessions; accept that bots verify mechanics, not the social game, and budget calendar time for human playtests accordingly.

topRisks.risk: Night-resolution engine correctness will be litigated by the community, and silent bugs are trust-fatal: in a deduction game, a wrong Sheriff result is indistinguishable from server cheating to the player. The published resolution order includes a 'repeat the Witch->BusDriver->Roleblocker cycle a random number of times' paradox solver, an acknowledged Jailor witch-immunity bug, and dozens of conversion/redirection edge cases documented only as wiki prose and forum rulings — a reimplementation from that material will diverge in ways veterans will catch in week one.
topRisks.mitigation: Write your own formal spec rather than transliterating the wiki; replace 'random number of iterations' with deterministic fixed-point iteration plus a documented tie-break; build an exhaustive interaction test suite seeded from the wiki edge cases (witch-on-witch, escort-blocks-escort-blocking-witch, MM-at-jailed-target); publish the resolution spec so the community debugs alongside you; expose per-match replays/audits from (seed, intents) so disputes resolve with evidence; decide explicitly, per mechanic, whether you want bug-for-bug fidelity or a clean fix, and document it.

topRisks.risk: Product-market contradiction the dossier states but never reconciles: its comps section proves the genre acquires players via streamers, built-in voice, and short clippable rounds — and the game being cloned is the exact opposite (text-only, 30-60 minute matches, dense jargon, dead players idling in a graveyard). Drifting into that gap means building a product with neither the niche depth veterans demand nor the casual funnel strangers need.
topRisks.mitigation: Force the positioning decision now: commit to being a niche community product for the text-mafia audience (MafiaScum/EpicMafia/SC2Mafia lineage), size expectations to a sustainable 100-500 CCU at near-zero burn, and lean into what that audience values — host tools, setup sharing, spectating, replays, private lobbies. Still ship a spectator/streamer mode (hide own-role/whispers from capture) and make trial/execution moments visually clippable, because streamer waves are free re-seeding even for niche titles (Feign's Turkish-streamer cycles).

topRisks.risk: Scope blowout. Even the 15-role MVP plus the setup editor, per-role option toggles, four day types, trials, whispers, wills, reconnection, moderation tooling, bot/test harness, and the Steam pipeline is realistically 12-24 months solo; the full 60-role surface with Cult conversion bookkeeping, Triad, and the option matrix is multi-year. First Steam release + first multiplayer game + first game ever is a compounding-unknowns stack.
topRisks.mitigation: Cut below the dossier's MVP: one day type (Majority + Trial), 2-3 fixed curated setups instead of the custom editor, 9-12 players; ship the setup editor and option toggles as the post-launch retention beat (they're also the features that multiply the QA matrix); hold Triad/Cult/Bus Driver/Witch until the game is live and stable; timebox a playable 9-player vertical slice (lobby -> roles -> day/vote/trial -> night -> win check) in 6-8 weeks as a go/no-go checkpoint.

topRisks.risk: The real legal threat is takedown asymmetry, not a lawsuit. The dossier's 'approximately zero' Blizzard-risk conclusion is sound, but a cheap Steam complaint — from BlankMediaGames on look-and-feel, 2K on the 'Mafia' video-game trademark, or even a troll — can delist a live multiplayer game for weeks during dispute resolution, which is fatal to a small population even when you'd ultimately win.
topRisks.mitigation: Pick an original title with distance from both 'SC2' and standalone 'Mafia'; build a theme visually distinct from both StarCraft and Town of Salem's Salem trade dress; rename the distinctive-tier roles (Triad set, Beguiler, Auditor) as the dossier says; document the clean-room process (sources used, no extracted assets) contemporaneously; have a counter-notice template and a games-IP lawyer contact ready before launch, not after the takedown lands.

topRisks.risk: Moderation and child-safety load on one person. Accusation-as-core-loop chat plus minors plus (likely) free accounts creates real obligations — DSA notice-and-action, and the UK Online Safety Act duties the dossier omits entirely — and a solo dev cannot staff a 72-hour human review queue at any traction level. EpicMafia died of governance, not technology; that lesson cuts against both no-moderation and hastily-deputized volunteer moderation.
topRisks.mitigation: Build the data model day one (reports, sanctions, append-only match_events — the dossier is right here) but phase the ceremony with scale; automate first: server-side evasion-aware filtering, rate limits, heuristic flags; when volunteers become necessary, give them scoped, fully-logged tools and a removal process (the EpicMafia failure was unaccountable mods); add an age gate and consider restricted chat defaults for minors; read the OSA's small-service duties before launch since UK players are inevitable.

topRisks.risk: Platform fragility in the recommended stack: steamworks.js is effectively single-maintainer with 67 open issues; the Steam overlay is broken on macOS and flaky on Windows for Electron; Steam Deck runs the Windows Electron build under Proton where a text-input-heavy game is borderline; and the dossier cites Valve C++ API features (FilterText, ShowFloatingGamepadTextInput, ICheatReportingService) without verifying the JS binding actually exposes them.
topRisks.mitigation: Wrap all Steamworks access behind a thin adapter so swapping to a fork or raw steamworks-rs is a contained change; keep Steam surface area minimal (auth tickets, achievements, rich presence — the dossier's own advice); spike-test the specific binding calls you depend on in week one, not at integration time; route invites through Steam-client launch args from the start instead of fighting the overlay; target Deck 'Playable' at most and don't spend MVP time on controller UI.

topRisks.risk: Off-platform collusion and dead-chat omniscience break stranger matches by design: friends in Discord voice sharing roles is technically unsolvable, and SC2Mafia's dead players see ALL hidden information — one dead friend in a voice call ruins the game for the living. Ranked integrity (win-trading, gamethrowing, multi-accounting, the Jester/thrower ambiguity) has no concrete design anywhere in the dossier.
topRisks.mitigation: Make dead-player information visibility a per-mode setting: full omniscience in private lobbies (it's fun with friends), restricted-until-game-end in matchmade games; accept collusion in private lobbies as out of scope; defer ranked entirely (see pushback) but log everything now so behavioral detection (vote-pattern anomalies, premature-knowledge tells) is possible later; treat 'reported for gamethrowing' as the dominant report category it will be and design the triage UI for it.

topRisks.risk: Browser+Steam dual-SKU complexity arrives earlier than the dossier admits: two distribution channels mean identity unification (SteamID vs email/web accounts), version skew between always-fresh browser clients and Steam-updated desktop clients hitting one server fleet, double the cheat/abuse surface (devtools-open browser client makes scripted clients trivial), and running two release pipelines as one person.
topRisks.mitigation: One account system from day one with Steam as a linked auth provider rather than a parallel identity; server-enforced protocol version with a force-refresh/update message; sequence rather than parallelize — browser-first launch, Steam SKU only after traction — so you never operate both channels before product-market fit; assume hostile scripted clients from the start (the server-authoritative design already covers correctness; add rate limiting and account-quality gates for abuse).

missingConsiderations: Phase-timer client sync and deadline races: server-side timers are specified, but not countdown drift correction on clients, what happens to a vote/night-action packet that arrives 200ms after phase cutoff (need an authoritative grace-window policy), 'Trial Pauses Day' timer arithmetic, or re-sync after tab sleep/background throttling in the browser build.

AFK/leaver design depth: does leaving reveal your role (information leak either way — SC2Mafia 'suicides' the leaver but their queued kill still lands)? Role-dodge quitting right after assignment, AFK detection escalation (default action -> seat kill -> bot replacement?), lobby ready-checks, and a leaver-penalty system. All of this hits in the first week of human playtests and none is specified.

Lobby host powers and migration: host disconnect during setup/naming phase, the -repick vote, kick/ban from lobby, and host griefing via degenerate setups in public lobbies (the SC2Mafia 'save built offline because lobbies get impatient' etiquette is itself a UX failure to fix, e.g. setup browser/vetted presets, not replicate).

Variable player-count support: every SC2Mafia setup assumes 15 players; matchmade reality is 7-12. Auto-scaling role lists with balance rules per count is a significant missing design system, and the single biggest lever against the cold-start problem.

Bots as two separate problems: scripted bots for testing (achievable, essential) versus bots for lobby backfill (a social deduction bot that chats convincingly is out of solo scope; LLM bots bring cost, latency, and moderation risk). The dossier should not let backfill bots be assumed as a cold-start solution.

Steam Playtest and Next Fest are absent from the shipping steps — Steam Playtest is the canonical free mechanism for pre-launch multiplayer testing at scale, and a Next Fest demo is the main wishlist-building event for an unknown multiplayer title.

New-player onboarding: this is a 60-role jargon-dense genre (N1, WIFOM, claims) and the dossier has zero on tutorialization — in-game role cards, contextual ability help, a bots-only tutorial match, glossary, simplified default setups for new accounts. Onboarding is the genre's biggest funnel filter.

Art and asset budget: nothing in the profile suggests art skills, and the legal analysis demands an original visual identity. Capsule art, role icons, execution animations, store assets, and any cosmetics pipeline must be contracted — unbudgeted money and schedule, and 'original look and feel' is precisely the legal mitigation, so it can't be skipped.

The monetization decision for THIS game is never actually made: comps conclude 'free or under $5, never gate matches,' but the dossier ends without a recommendation. F2P on Steam invites the bot/ban-evasion problems the dossier itself documents (Among Us, ToS1); paid suppresses the population it can't afford to lose. This is a core open decision, not a detail.

Deploy/ops with live games: you cannot restart the room server mid-match. Needs graceful drain (stop allocating new rooms, wait out running games), per-process room sharding or blue-green from day one, and a stated crash-recovery policy — the dossier calls event-log recovery a 'nice-to-have,' which stops being true the day real users exist.

Localization and language-split lobbies: chat-based deduction is unplayable cross-language, so the lobby list/queue must segment by language; the Feign lesson implies deliberately picking one or two launch languages and owning those communities. String externalization is near-free in the web stack if done from day one, expensive retrofitted.

Accessibility specifics: faction identity is literally red/green (colorblind-hostile — needs shapes/labels), text scaling, keyboard-only play, reduced-motion for execution sequences, and screen-reader-friendly DOM — the last being a genuine web-stack advantage no engine competitor can match, worth exploiting deliberately.

Telemetry and population health instrumentation: lobby wait time, match completion rate, first-session retention, geographic/timezone concentration — the comps explicitly say 'alive only at 7pm EST' is the death-spiral early-warning, but the dossier specs no analytics to detect it.

Spectator mode and a replay viewer as concrete scoped features: the event log enables them, but the UI is real work; also a streamer-safety mode (hide own role/whispers from capture until reveal) given streamability is the genre's only free acquisition channel.

Chat infrastructure mundanities: per-channel rate limiting, paste-flood and mention spam control, link/markup sanitization (the Godot section worries about BBCode injection but the web stack has its own XSS-in-chat surface), whisper metadata rules, persistent client-side mutes.

Verification that steamworks.js exposes the specific APIs the plan leans on (FilterText, ShowFloatingGamepadTextInput, overlay-invite flows) — the dossier cites Valve's C++ documentation throughout but never checks binding coverage; ICheatReportingService game bans are a server-side Web API call and fine, but client-side surface needs a spike.

Marketing beyond shipping mechanics: the Steam section covers how to ship, not how anyone finds out — wishlist campaign, dev-logging to the SC2Mafia/ToS diaspora (Reddit r/TownofSalem2, sc2mafia forum remnants, UltiMafia Discord), browser-portal distribution (itch.io, CrazyGames) for the web client, and the explicit 'why switch from free UltiMafia/ToS2' differentiation argument, which the dossier never makes.

Bug-for-bug fidelity vs clean redesign as an explicit, documented per-mechanic decision (Jailor witch-immunity bug, random-iteration paradox solver, Triad-beats-Mafia tie rules): veterans will demand fidelity, newcomers won't care, and drifting silently between the two produces the worst of both.
pushback: Steam-first sequencing is wrong-ordered relative to the dossier's own best insight. If the browser version is the population-seeding strategy, it should LAUNCH first — Steam 6-12 months later once nightly lobbies demonstrably fill. The Steam release is a one-shot visibility event (new-release feed, first reviews); burning it on empty lobbies converts the cold-start problem into permanent 'dead game' reviews. The 4-6 week Steam pipeline and $100 fee should wait for traction, not anchor the plan.

macOS effort is heavily overweighted: $99/yr Apple Developer, notarization yak-shaving, entitlements gotchas — for a platform that is single-digit-percent of this audience, where the Steam overlay is broken anyway, and which the browser build covers completely. Ship Windows+web at launch; add the Mac depot post-traction if Mac players actually materialize.

Colyseus StateView is oversold as the security lever. Tagging fields to hide is a blacklist model; for hidden-information secrecy you want whitelist-by-default — explicit per-client event sends where nothing reaches a socket unless deliberately addressed to it. That's trivially built on plain ws + zod with the dev's existing skills, and the 'you'd rebuild 60% of Colyseus' claim is inflated: the hard 60% (phase state machine, night resolution, per-client filtering discipline) is game-specific and yours to write regardless. Colyseus is a fine convenience choice; it is not what makes the game cheat-proof, and boardgame.io's own secrets-leaked-via-side-paths issue (#399) shows why send-discipline beats field-tagging.

Glicko-2/ranked at launch is premature and mildly harmful: a ranked queue splits an already-thin population, and the dossier has no answer for win-trading, multi-accounting, or gamethrowing detection that ranked immediately invites. Launch unranked with visible stats; add ratings when CCU can support split queues. Keep the rating_before/rating_after schema columns — recomputable later from the event log anyway.

The 15-player, 15-slot frame should not survive contact with launch reality: filling 15 strangers is brutal at realistic launch CCU. Make 9-12 the designed default with auto-scaling setups and let 15 be the community-event format. Same pushback applies to the option matrix — 4 day types x 3 night types x dozens of per-role toggles exists because SC2 Arcade hosts had captive lobbies; quickmatch strangers need 2-3 curated setups, and every toggle multiplies a QA matrix one person cannot cover. Ship the configurator late as a retention feature, not early as a foundation.

The packet-size/timing side-channel padding advice is over-engineering for MVP: traffic-shape analysis to infer faction is a threat worth a backlog note, not launch work, for a sub-1k-CCU text game. Need-to-know serialization is the 99% defense; do that and move on.

The DSA-shaped moderation prescription is compliance-overweight pre-traction: build the data model (reports, sanctions, evidence-linked event log) from day one — that part is correct and cheap — but a 72h human-review SLA and formal Article 16 notice flows for a game with 50 CCU is ceremony; a working server-side mute, a filter, and a Discord channel is the honest launch bar, with the formal machinery phased in as user counts justify it. Meanwhile the dossier omits the UK Online Safety Act, which in 2026 is arguably the more aggressive regime for a small chat platform.

The comps section's scaling lessons (Unity Multiplay, elastic capacity 'ready before the viral moment') are mostly inapplicable and risk infra-anxiety spending: a text-mafia niche title will not 10,000x overnight, and if lightning somehow strikes, a room-based architecture shards horizontally fast enough. One box plus a tested drain-and-shard plan is genuinely sufficient; resist pre-buying for a spike that will not come.

Hosting cost analysis prices the VPS but not the human: the binding constraint on a solo live-service operator is attention — on-call, moderation, community management, content cadence — which argues for the most boring possible stack (fewer moving parts beats framework features) and for designing community self-service (host tools, volunteer-runnable events) as load-shedding, not just as features.

The dossier's two strongest sections argue against its implicit ambition and nobody calls it: the comps prove this genre rewards either viral casual products (voice, short rounds, streamable) or zero-burn community platforms (BYO-group, hostable, open-ish) — and punishes everything in between. A faithful SC2Mafia clone is structurally the second thing. The plan should explicitly embrace hobby-business economics (sub-$5 or free, ~100-500 CCU ceiling, near-zero burn, community-as-infrastructure) or explicitly diverge from the source design toward voice/short-rounds — the dossier currently lets him believe he can split the difference.

'Approximately zero' legal risk conflates probability with severity: the realistic vector is a cheap takedown complaint (BMG look-and-feel, 2K's 'Mafia' mark) delisting a population-dependent live game for weeks during dispute — low probability, but the mitigation (naming distance, theme distance, documented clean-room, counter-notice readiness) costs almost nothing and should be framed as mandatory, not optional polish.

Trusting the dossier's Steamworks feature analysis without a binding spike is a trap: it consistently cites Valve's C++ API docs (lobbies, FilterText, floating keyboard, rich presence connect keys) while the actual dependency is steamworks.js's coverage of those calls in Electron. Week-one task: a throwaway Electron app exercising every Steam call the plan needs, on Windows and on a Deck, before any architecture hardens around them.
